qs.q: How does lysogenic conversion affect a host bacterium such as Corynebacterium diphtheriae?
o: It grants the bacterium traits like diphtheria toxin production
It converts the bacterial chromosome into a segmented RNA
It destroys the host cell via rapid lytic replication
It permanently prevents any future bacteriophage infections
qs.e: Lysogenic conversion occurs when a prophage imparts new genetic traits to the host bacterium, such as the tox gene required for Corynebacterium diphtheriae to produce diphtheria toxin. The lytic cycle, rather than lysogenic conversion, destroys the host cell immediately.

qs.q: The presence of a pseudomembrane in the throat, a thick, grayish-white layer, is a hallmark of diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
qs.e: A pseudomembrane is a characteristic feature of diphtheria. It is formed by necrotic tissue, fibrin, and bacteria on the surface of the pharynx and tonsils. While severe strep throat can sometimes have exudates, a true pseudomembrane is indicative of diphtheria.

qs.q: The Elek test is used to detect toxigenicity of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It involves placing a filter paper strip soaked in antitoxin onto an agar plate inoculated with the bacterium. If the bacterium produces diphtheria toxin, a visible precipitation line will form where the toxin meets the antitoxin.
qs.e: The Elek test is a qualitative in vitro assay used to determine if a strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae is toxigenic (i.e., capable of producing diphtheria toxin). It is a serological test based on the precipitation reaction between the produced toxin and specific antitoxin.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Gram‑positive bacillus that, when lysogenised by a beta‑phage, produces diphtheria toxin causing a necrotising pseudomembrane in the throat and systemic toxin effects. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical picture and simple labs; antitoxin and antibiotics are lifesaving.

sections.p: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a non‑sporing, non‑motile, Gram‑positive rod that forms characteristic palisades (“Chinese letters”) on microscopy. Only toxigenic strains, which have acquired the tox gene from a lysogenic β‑phage, cause disease.
b: Toxigenic strains produce diphtheria toxin (an ADP‑ribosyltransferase).
Endemic in areas with low vaccination coverage; outbreaks still occur in East Africa.

sections.p: The bacterium grows on simple media such as tellurite agar, producing black colonies. It is catalase‑positive and ferments glucose without gas.
b: Gram‑positive rod, club‑shaped, forms metachromatic granules.
Requires iron‑limited environment for maximal toxin production.

sections.p: Spread is mainly via respiratory droplets or direct contact with contaminated objects. The organism colonises the nasopharynx; the phage‑encoded toxin is expressed after bacterial adherence.
b: Incubation 2–5 days; contagious until 48 h after antibiotics.
Carrier state possible, especially in unimmunised children.

sections.p: Classic diphtheria presents with a grey‑white pseudomembrane that adheres to the tonsils, pharynx or nasopharynx, causing airway obstruction and systemic toxin effects (myocarditis, neuropathy).
b: Local disease: sore throat, fever, cervical lymphadenopathy, bull neck.
Systemic toxin: myocarditis (arrhythmia, heart failure) and peripheral neuropathy (cranial nerves, then motor weakness).
Severe disease more common in children <5 yr, malnourished, HIV‑positive or with co‑existing TB.

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple laboratory tests when available.

t.a: Microscopy of a throat swab (Gram stain)
t.b: Confirms Gram‑positive rods; helps rule out other bacterial pharyngitis.
Black colonies suggest C. diphtheriae; if unavailable, skip to toxin testing.
Detects toxin production; if not available, treat as toxigenic based on clinical picture.
Rapid confirmation of toxigenic strain; not required for immediate management.

sections.p: Management is three‑pronged: neutralise circulating toxin, eradicate the organism, and prevent spread.
b: Diphtheria antitoxin (horse‑derived) – given as soon as suspicion arises; neutralises free toxin only.
Penicillin G or erythromycin – kills bacteria; erythromycin preferred if penicillin allergy.
Isolation, contact tracing, and booster DPT vaccine for contacts.

t.b: Give high‑dose erythromycin immediately; arrange transfer for antitoxin if possible.
Serial ECG and cardiac enzymes; treat arrhythmias per ACLS if they develop.

sections.p: Focus on the clinical picture, toxin pathophysiology, and urgent steps.
b: Pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal → classic sign.
‘Bull neck’ = massive cervical lymphadenopathy, a red‑flag for airway compromise.
Antitoxin must be given before antibiotics to avoid worsening toxin release.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding pseudomembrane causing airway obstruction
Signs of myocarditis (chest pain, arrhythmia, hypotension)
Neurological decline (cranial nerve palsy, limb weakness)

faq.q: Why does antitoxin not reverse tissue damage?
faq.a: It neutralises only circulating toxin; toxin already bound to cells causes irreversible necrosis.

faq.q: Can a non‑toxigenic strain cause disease?
faq.a: Rarely; disease severity is driven by toxin, so non‑toxigenic strains usually cause mild colonisation.

faq.q: What is the role of the DPT booster in contacts?
faq.a: It provides rapid protective antibodies and prevents secondary cases.

exam: A 4‑year‑old presents with a grey pseudomembrane and stridor – what is your immediate management and why? — Give antitoxin first, then start erythromycin; secure airway if needed.
How does the diphtheria toxin cause myocarditis? — ADP‑ribosylates EF‑2, halting protein synthesis, leading to cell death in cardiac myocytes.

Why is penicillin sometimes avoided in diphtheria patients? — In severe disease, rapid bacterial lysis may release more toxin; erythromycin is equally effective and less likely to cause Jarisch‑Herxheimer‑like reaction.

A patient cannot receive antitoxin due to severe serum sickness risk – what alternative steps? — Give high‑dose erythromycin, isolate, vaccinate contacts, and arrange transfer for antitoxin if possible.
What laboratory finding would mislead you into thinking the infection is viral? — Normal white‑cell count; remember diphtheria can present with modest leukocytosis.

How would you differentiate diphtheria from severe streptococcal pharyngitis in a setting without culture? — Presence of a tightly adherent grey‑white membrane that bleeds on removal, cervical ‘bull neck’, and systemic toxin signs.
Explain why a child with HIV is at higher risk of severe diphtheria. — Immunosuppression impairs clearance of bacteria and may allow higher toxin load.
What public‑health measure stops an outbreak in a refugee camp? — Mass DPT vaccination, chemoprophylaxis with erythromycin for close contacts, and strict isolation of cases.
